title: FRCP Expert Disclosure: Rule 26 Requirements and Checklist
summary: FRCP expert disclosure guide: learn who needs a Rule 26 report, what to include, when it is due, and how patent teams can reduce exclusion and sanctions risk.
body_markdown:
An expert disclosure sets out the opinions, evidence, and assumptions that can shape summary judgment and trial. A missed deadline or incomplete report can remove a technical theory from the case. The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (FRCP), particularly Rule 26, supply the baseline, while the scheduling order, local rules, standing orders, and stipulations usually supply the dates and added detail. Reconcile all of them before the expert starts writing. This is general information, not legal advice.


## Key takeaways


- **Every potential trial expert must be classified.** Retained experts and employees whose duties regularly involve expert testimony generally need a full Rule 26(a)(2)(B) report. For other testifying experts, the party generally provides a Rule 26(a)(2)(C) summary disclosure.
- **The case schedule controls.** The 90-day deadline for opening disclosures and 30-day period for rebuttal are defaults that apply only when no stipulation or court order sets another schedule.
- **A retained expert's report has six required components.** The expert must prepare and sign it. Completeness covers every opinion, its basis, facts or data considered, supporting exhibits, qualifications and publications, prior testimony, and compensation.
- **“Considered” reaches beyond “relied on.”** Facts or data considered in forming the opinions may require disclosure even if the expert did not rely on them.
- **Supplementation corrects the record.** Using it for a new theory that could have appeared in the opening or rebuttal report creates exclusion and sanctions risk.
- **Rule 37(c)(1) puts the merits at risk.** An undisclosed witness or opinion may be excluded from a motion, hearing, or trial unless the failure was substantially justified or harmless.


## What is an FRCP expert disclosure?


An FRCP expert disclosure is the written identification and required supporting information for any witness a party may use at trial to present expert evidence under Federal Rules of Evidence 702, 703, or 705. Rule 26(a)(2) divides those witnesses into two disclosure tracks.


The first track is a full written report under Rule 26(a)(2)(B). The second is a shorter summary under Rule 26(a)(2)(C). The[current federal rule](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf) also governs timing, supplementation, expert discovery, draft protection, and protected attorney-expert communications.


A consulting expert who is not expected to testify falls outside the trial-witness disclosure requirement. Rule 26(b)(4)(D) ordinarily protects that expert's facts and opinions from discovery, subject to the rule's exceptions. Once a team may use the expert's opinion at trial, the disclosure analysis changes.


## Which expert disclosure does the witness need?


Start with the witness's role and expected testimony. Job title alone does not decide the issue. The categories below apply unless the court orders or the parties stipulate otherwise.


Witness Rule 26 treatment Required disclosure


Expert retained or specially employed to testify in the case Rule 26(a)(2)(B) Identity plus a prepared and signed written report containing all six required categories


Party employee whose duties regularly involve giving expert testimony Rule 26(a)(2)(B) Identity plus the same full written report


Testifying expert outside those report categories, often a treating professional or employee with firsthand technical knowledge Rule 26(a)(2)(C) Identity, subject matter, and a summary of the facts and opinions expected at trial


Consulting expert who will not testify Rule 26(b)(4)(D) No Rule 26(a)(2) trial disclosure, unless the role changes or the court orders otherwise


Patent cases make the employee category easy to mishandle. An inventor, engineer, product manager, or technical employee may have percipient knowledge and enough specialized knowledge to offer an expert opinion. If the party may use that person to present Rule 702, 703, or 705 evidence, the person needs an expert disclosure even if a full report is unnecessary.


Employee status also needs evidentiary support. In *Tokai Corp. v. Easton Enterprises* , a patent owner tried to use declarations from technical witnesses without reports. The[Federal Circuit affirmed](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/10-1057.pdf) exclusion after the patent owner failed to establish that an asserted employee qualified for the report exception and failed to justify its disclosure decision.


### What a Rule 26(a)(2)(C) summary must say


A summary disclosure for a non-reporting expert must identify:


1. The subject matter of the expected expert evidence.
2. A summary of the facts and opinions the witness is expected to give.


A name, job description, document dump, or broad reservation of testimony does not perform that work. The summary should tell opposing counsel what the witness will opine and which matter-specific facts support each opinion. It can remain materially shorter than a retained expert's report.


## Rule 26(a)(2)(B) expert report checklist


The six rule categories are a floor. A technically complete package can still fail if its opinions are conclusory or its reasoning is impossible to follow.


Required component Completeness check


Complete statement of opinions, bases, and reasons Connect each opinion to the reasoning the expert expects to give on direct examination. In a patent case, identify the claim, limitation, construction, reference, product feature, or damages input at issue.


Facts or data considered Maintain an inventory of the factual material the expert considered in forming the opinions, including material considered and rejected. Preserve document identifiers, versions, dates, pinpoint locations, and the relationship to an opinion.


Exhibits used to summarize or support opinions Include each chart, calculation, figure, model, or demonstrative the expert expects to use for support or summary. Check that its labels and source citations match the report.


Witness qualifications and 10-year publication list Describe the witness's qualifications, including education, training, and experience relevant to the opinions. A current curriculum vitae can supply those details, but the rule expressly requires the qualifications, including a list of all publications the witness authored in the previous 10 years. Reconcile inconsistent titles, coauthors, and dates.


Four-year testimony list Include every case in which the witness testified as an expert at trial or deposition during the previous four years. Add caption, court, case number, and trial or deposition status where a local rule or order requires that detail.


Compensation statement State the compensation for study and testimony in this engagement, including the applicable rates or fee arrangement. Align it with the engagement letter and invoices.


The report must be prepared and signed by the witness. Counsel may assist with organization, legal standards, citations, and editing, but the final opinions and reasoning must be the expert's. The expert should be able to explain the report's language, calculations, selected evidence, and omissions without adopting counsel's reasoning for the first time at deposition.


### Completeness is substantive in patent cases


An invalidity report that lists references and ends with an obviousness conclusion leaves out the reasoning the rule is designed to disclose. The[Federal Circuit explained](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/11-1329.pdf) in *Meyer Intellectual Properties Ltd. v. Bodum, Inc.* that an expert should state how or why a person of ordinary skill would reach the asserted obviousness result from the identified references.


The same principle applies to infringement and noninfringement. An infringement opinion should map each limitation of the asserted claim to the accused product or process under the governing construction. A noninfringement opinion should identify each limitation on which the conclusion rests and explain why the accused product or process does not meet it. A citation list, claim chart, or declaration cannot preserve an unstated opinion by implication.


In *Trudell Medical International Inc. v. D R Burton Healthcare, LLC* , the[Federal Circuit held](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/23-1777.OPINION.2-7-2025_2465245.pdf) that undisclosed noninfringement testimony should have been excluded. The witness's trial testimony also exceeded the scope of his declaration because it addressed a claim limitation the declaration did not discuss.


## When are expert disclosures due under FRCP 26?


Expert disclosures are due when the court orders. Read the scheduling order together with amendments, local rules, patent local rules, standing orders, and stipulations. Rule 16(b)(4) allows a schedule to be modified only for good cause and with the judge's consent, so a private team plan cannot move the operative deadline.


If no order or stipulation sets the timing, Rule 26(a)(2)(D) supplies these defaults:


- **Opening expert disclosure:** At least 90 days before the date set for trial or for the case to be ready for trial.
- **Rebuttal expert disclosure:** Within 30 days after the other party's disclosure, when the evidence is intended solely to contradict or rebut evidence on the same subject matter.


The word “solely” gives the rebuttal deadline a narrow job. A party should develop its affirmative theories for the opening report rather than reserve them for rebuttal. A case-specific order may also authorize reply reports, prescribe topic sequencing, set separate damages dates, or limit the number of experts.


Patent local rules can add a second expert-report track well before merits reports. Under the Northern District of California's[Patent Local Rule 4-3](https://cand.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/local-rules/Patent_Local_Rules_08-11-2026.pdf) , unless the parties agree otherwise, a party that intends to rely on a witness's expert testimony to support its proposed claim constructions must serve the other party or parties with a Rule 26(a)(2)(B)-compliant report for that witness no later than 60 days after service of the invalidity contentions.


*Northern District of California Patent L.R. 4-3, revised August 11, 2026.*


Build the internal schedule backward from service. Leave time for the expert's final source review, calculations, quality control, signature, service package, and a failure buffer. Opening-report work also needs to respect contention deadlines. An invalidity or infringement theory omitted from timely contentions may draw a motion to strike or exclusion under the applicable patent local rules.


## How to prepare and serve a defensible disclosure


### 1. Build the control sheet


Collect every source of operative requirements in one place. Record opening, opposition, rebuttal, reply, deposition, supplementation, and motion deadlines. Add page limits, required testimony-list fields, service method, confidentiality designations, and dispute procedures.


### 2. Classify witnesses and assign issues


Create a witness matrix before drafting. For each witness, record the expected Rule 702 subject, opinion scope, retained or employee status, report category, and assigned issues. In a patent case, map ownership for claim construction, infringement, invalidity, damages, source code, surveys, and secondary considerations.


### 3. Lock the opinion architecture


Outline every opinion at the level opposing counsel will test it. Link the conclusion to the legal question, technical reasoning, facts or data, assumptions, and exhibits. Reconcile that architecture with pleadings, contentions, interrogatory responses, claim constructions, admissions, and the evidentiary record.


### 4. Control the considered-materials record


Use a stable repository for documents sent to or reviewed by the expert. Track version, date, source, and review status. This reduces disputes over what the expert considered and prevents a citation from pointing to a superseded claim chart, source-code excerpt, product manual, or damages calculation.


### 5. Run a cross-document audit


Check every report statement against its source. Then compare the report to exhibits, appendices, curriculum vitae, publication list, testimony list, compensation terms, and calculations. For patent reports, confirm claim numbers, limitation labels, constructions, priority dates, product versions, reference dates, pinpoint citations, and consistent terminology.


Our guide to[submission-ready claim charts](https://www.tryandai.com/blog/submission-ready-claim-charts-with-ai) explains the same source-to-citation discipline for limitation-level work product. A chart can organize support for the expert, while the report still needs the expert's complete opinion and reasoning.


### 6. Obtain signatures and serve the package


Rule 26(a)(4) requires disclosures to be written, signed, and served. The retained expert signs the report. Preserve the final served files, exhibits, service correspondence, and hash or version record so the team can identify the exact disclosure used at deposition.


Rule 5(d)(1)(A) ordinarily keeps Rule 26(a)(2) disclosures off the docket until they are used in the proceeding or the court orders filing. A local rule or case-specific order can change the filing workflow.


## What is protected, and what is discoverable?


Rule 26 protects drafts of both reports and summary disclosures, regardless of the form in which the draft was recorded. It also protects communications between counsel and a witness required to provide a Rule 26(a)(2)(B) report, with three express exceptions. Discovery can reach the portions of communications that:


- Relate to compensation for the expert's study or testimony.
- Identify facts or data counsel provided and the expert considered in forming the opinions to be expressed.
- Identify assumptions counsel provided and the expert relied on in forming the opinions to be expressed.


The final report must disclose facts or data the expert considered in forming the opinions to be expressed even when the expert did not ultimately rely on them. Keep that distinction visible when managing email, shared workspaces, annotations, and source packets. Draft protection does not shrink the considered-materials obligation.


Once a report is provided, the opposing party may depose the expert. Rule 26(b)(4)(A) delays the deposition of a report witness until after the report has been supplied, giving the report its intended role as the roadmap for expert discovery.


## Supplementation and the cost of getting disclosure wrong


Rule 26(e) requires a timely correction when a disclosure is materially incomplete or incorrect and the new information has not otherwise been made known during discovery or in writing. For a report witness, the duty covers both the report and deposition testimony. Additions or changes must be disclosed by the Rule 26(a)(3) pretrial-disclosure deadline, unless the court orders another date.


That outer deadline does not make supplementation a low-risk reserve round of expert briefing. Rule 26(e) does not state that every new opinion is categorically barred. In practice, material that looks like a theory that should have appeared in the opening or rebuttal report can draw a motion to strike or exclude, especially when the information was available before the original deadline. A correction should identify what changed, why the earlier statement became incomplete or incorrect, and which opinions or materials are affected.


The[Rule 37(c)(1) sanction](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf) supplies the direct consequence. A party that fails to provide required information or identify a witness cannot use the information or witness to supply evidence on a motion, at a hearing, or at trial unless the failure was substantially justified or harmless. In addition to or instead of exclusion, the court may, on motion and after giving an opportunity to be heard, order payment of the reasonable expenses and attorney's fees caused by the failure, inform the jury of the failure, or impose other appropriate sanctions, including the orders listed in Rule 37(b)(2)(A)(i) through (vi).
